passages.text: Grokking describes understanding something deeply and intuitively. In neural networks, it is the phenomenon where a network generalizes long after memorizing its training data. This delay has been linked to a fall in the effective rank of the network’s weight matrices, but whether this rank compression drives grokking or follows it is still unresolved. We study a mean-field MLP and a one-layer transformer trained on modular arithmetic and observe that: (i) Compression follows the onset, not memorization. Every transformer memorizes its training data within 250 steps, while the grokking onset (the first step at which test accuracy reaches 95%) varies from 6,500 to 21,000 steps. The steepest fall in effective rank comes about 900 steps after the onset, however late the onset occurs, and networks that memorize without grokking compress far less. (ii) Subspace crystallization. We call the span of the fewest top singular directions of a weight matrix that preserve 99% of test accuracy its sufficient subspace . Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route tokens unevenly across experts, creating time-varying optimization conditions [ 1 ] . This setting can be challenging for Muon-family optimizers, which use Newton–Schulz (NS) iterations to transform momentum-based updates. Muon has shown promise for language-model pretraining [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] , while Hyperball introduces explicit control over weight and update norms [ 5 ] . Its Muon variant, MuonH, normalizes update directions and projects weights onto a fixed-radius sphere. In our custom 4B-parameter DeepSeekMoE-style model, both Muon and MuonH exhibit intermittent loss spikes, although all full-schedule runs complete. We investigate whether these loss excursions can be mitigated through a simple modification of routed-expert updates.

An expert can retain nonzero momentum even when no tokens are assigned to it in the current step. This motivates examining expert-wise update magnitudes, particularly under MuonH’s fixed-norm normalization. We propose EnergyCal, a lightweight rule that attenuates each routed-expert update according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of its finite-step NS direction. Figure 1 illustrates the method. The coefficient is bounded between zero and one and is applied continuously during training. EnergyCal leaves the NS transform, momentum, and router objective unchanged, requires no token-utilization statistics, and adds no persistent optimizer state. Its energy statistic is not scale-invariant stable rank: low energy can reflect direction concentration, amplitude, or both. We evaluate EnergyCal in two separate full-schedule studies, each using three initialization seeds. First, a frozen EnergyCal–MuonH recipe reduces mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06% relative to a development-selected, lower-learning-rate MuonH recipe, with 1.62% lower mean throughput. Second, applying EnergyCal to plain Muon at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay reduces mean spike burden by 95.98% on average across the two tested exponents, with small endpoint improvements. Together, these results show that stabilization is observed both with and without Hyperball in the evaluated MoE setting. However, plain Muon retains intermediate-quality and speed advantages in the first study, and different evaluation banks prevent a direct ranking of the calibrated optimizer families.

The success of large language models in real-world applications relies on parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ), which inserts compact, trainable adapters into selected layers. In this paper, we propose SimplexLoRA , a LoRA variant that adaptively adjusts adapter ranks during fine-tuning based on their learned importance. Unlike standard LoRA , which employs a fixed rank across all layers, SimplexLoRA optimizes per-adapter importance weights on the n n -scaled simplex during a short warm-up and then freezes them, dynamically allocating capacity where it is most beneficial without increasing the overall parameter budget or inference cost. We evaluate SimplexLoRA across 12 language understanding, summarization, and reasoning tasks using DeBERTaV3, BART-large, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen3-8B. Our results show that SimplexLoRA consistently matches or outperforms standard LoRA and recent adaptive baselines, with the largest gains at low ranks. Our code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SimplexLoRA .

LoRA [ Hu et al., 2021 ] is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method [ Han et al., 2024 ] that parameterizes weight updates as 𝑾 ′ = 𝑾 0 + 𝑨 ​ 𝑩 {\bm{W}}^{\prime}={\bm{W}}^{0}+{\bm{A}}{\bm{B}} , with 𝑾 0 ∈ ℝ m × d {\bm{W}}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} frozen and trainable 𝑨 ∈ ℝ m × r , 𝑩 ∈ ℝ r × d {\bm{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},{\bm{B}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} , r ≪ m , d r\ll m,d . This approach achieves low inference overhead and substantially reduces memory during fine-tuning. Figure 1: SimplexLoRA framework. Per-adapter importance weights are constrained to the n n -scaled simplex, enabling dynamic allocation of a fixed rank budget across layers. Despite its efficiency, standard LoRA uses a fixed rank across all layers, ignoring layer-wise differences in convergence and representation learning. Existing adaptive rank allocation methods attempt to address this issue but suffer from the critical drawbacks: (i) substantially more trainable parameters [ Sheng et al., 2025 ] , (ii) non-negligible inference-time overhead caused by dynamic pruning or gating mechanisms [ Zhang et al., 2025 ] , and (iii) deviations from the standard LoRA pipeline that hinder compatibility [ Zhang et al., 2023b ] . See Section 2 for further discussion. To address this limitation, we propose SimplexLoRA , which assigns an importance weight to each of the n n LoRA adapters, constrained to the n n -scaled simplex to enforce a fixed parameter budget. Key properties: (i) ranks learned automatically during fine-tuning; (ii) simplex constraint preserves the LoRA parameter budget; (iii) full LoRA compatibility; (iv) negligible training and inference overhead.

While LoRA has popularized parameter-efficient fine-tuning, it is not the only method to explore low-rank or structured adaptations. Earlier approaches include LoHA [ Nam et al., 2022 ] , which utilizes element-wise (Hadamard) interactions between low-rank matrices to reduce the parameter count without sacrificing expressivity, and Krona [ Edalati et al., 2022 ] , which employs the Kronecker product in place of the conventional low-rank matrix product to improve parameter efficiency while maintaining model capacity. Subsequent methods extended or refined the LoRA framework. VERA [ Kopiczko et al., 2023 ] reduces adapter storage by sharing frozen random projection matrices across layers and learning small scaling vectors. rsLoRA [ Kalajdzievski, 2023 ] replaces the original LoRA scaling factor α / r \alpha/r [ Hu et al., 2021 ] with the rank-stabilized factor α / r \alpha/\sqrt{r} . A complementary direction is taken by DoRA [ Liu et al., 2024 ] , which decomposes the adapted weight into magnitude and direction components and learns the magnitude together with a low-rank correction of the direction. Another line of work improves LoRA optimization and numerical efficiency. LoRA+ [ Hayou et al., 2024 ] uses different learning rates for the two adapter matrices, while QLoRA [ Dettmers et al., 2023 ] enables memory-efficient fine-tuning through 4-bit quantization of frozen base-model weights. Both are orthogonal to our adaptive rank allocation method and can be combined with it.

Across most GLUE tasks, SimplexLoRA consistently outperforms LoRA while maintaining the same computational cost. For generality, we also evaluate Qwen3-8B (GSM8K, BoolQ, HellaSwag) and BART-large (XSum, CNN/DailyMail) in Table 3 . As on GLUE, SimplexLoRA matches or outperforms LoRA on most of these tasks, confirming the trend across architectures and task types. The improvement is most pronounced at low ranks ( r ∈ { 1 , 2 } r\in\{1,2\} ), where the tight capacity budget of standard LoRA gives adaptive allocation the most room to help. We presented SimplexLoRA , a LoRA variant that allocates a fixed rank budget non-uniformly across layers via short alternating optimization on the n n -scaled simplex. Across 12 tasks and four backbones up to 8B parameters, SimplexLoRA matches or outperforms standard LoRA and recent adaptive baselines at the same parameter count and inference cost, with the largest gains in the low-rank regime.

The limitations of the proposed strategy are as follows. First, SimplexLoRA introduces three additional hyperparameters: the number of iterations between simplex projection steps T T , the total number of such projections K K , and the weight decay coefficient used for regularization; the ablation in Section 4.3 indicates that the method is robust within a broad range but does not eliminate the need to set these values. Second, the lack of experiments on models substantially larger than 8B parameters limits the generalizability of our findings. Third, while the per-task averages over three seeds consistently favor SimplexLoRA , on a few individual tasks (e.g., CoLA and RTE in the out-of-the-box DeBERTaV3 comparison) standard LoRA remains competitive or slightly better, indicating that the benefit of adaptive rank allocation is task-dependent. Fourth, a fundamental ambiguity remains during training: a small gradient norm in a layer may indicate either that the weights are well-optimized or that the gradients have vanished by the time they reach that layer, which can in principle bias the learned importance weights. On the ethical side, we see no specific risks beyond those already inherent to fine-tuning large language models: this work studies a parameter-efficient adaptation procedure, introduces no new data sources, uses only publicly available benchmarks with no proprietary or personal data and no human subjects, and reduces rather than increases the compute and memory footprint of fine-tuning.

passages.text: Large language models have rapidly become a powerful tool for relevance ranking, where a single model is prompted with a query alongside an ordered list of candidate passages and asked to directly emit the permutation that best reflects their relevance ( Sun et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2023 ; liu2026training ) . This listwise formulation lets the model reason jointly over all candidates and exploit cross-passage comparisons that pointwise and pairwise scorers cannot capture, and it has proven so effective that the capability of proprietary models has been distilled into compact open-source rankers that now serve as strong and reproducible baselines ( Pradeep et al., 2023a ; Pradeep et al., 2023b ) . Driven by these successes, listwise ranking with large language models has quickly become a central paradigm in modern retrieval pipelines. However, in web search and retrieval-augmented applications, the response must also be produced within an inference budget. A conventional listwise reranker serializes the candidate passages into the ranking prompt. Its input grows with both the number and length of passages, even when the entire list fits inside the model’s context window ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . A long candidate list, or passages that are individually long, quickly inflates inference latency, degrading both ranking quality and responsiveness. As shown in Figure 1 , the prevailing remedy is to process the list through a sliding window that reranks overlapping blocks and propagates the ordering across passes ( Sun et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025d ) , but this comes at the cost of repeatedly re-encoding overlapping content. These costs motivate reducing the information consumed by the ranking stage, while explicitly accounting for any work needed to prepare that information.

Figure 1: Comparison of existing listwise ranking strategies: Sliding Window, Full Ranking and GistRank , corresponding to panels (a), (b), and (c), respectively. A promising solution is to compress each passage before ranking, for example, extracting a summary or embedding the passage ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . Besides, a family of soft-compression methods encodes long inputs into a handful of trainable gist tokens that retain the conditioning effect of the original text while drastically shortening the sequence ( Mu et al., 2023 ; Ge et al., 2023 ) . We argue that such compression is a natural fit for improving inference efficiency in ranking tasks, as it could replace each verbatim passage with a compact set of gist tokens. Prior work has in fact measured gist and KV-level compression on reranking and reported a large gap to full attention ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , but has treated that gap as an intrinsic cost of compression. We argue it is instead a feature of the compression objective: relevance judgment hinges on fine-grained, query-conditioned distinctions among closely competing candidates, whereas objectives optimised for reconstruction or generative conditioning are never asked to preserve those distinctions. In ranking, the compressed states must expose relative preference across candidates, not merely preserve a useful account of each passage. Bridging this gap therefore requires adapting the gist representation so that it preserves the discriminative signals on which ranking depends.

We propose GistRank , which equips a large language model with compressed gist tokes passage representations for efficiency listwise ranking through a three-stage training procedure. In the first stage, we learn faithful gist representations: fixed-length documents are followed by a set of gist tokens that are in turn concatenated with the query, with the query trailing the gist tokens. The model is trained to predict the subsequent tokens conditioned solely on the gist, while granting the gist tokens richer bidirectional access to their source context. In the second stage, with the gist tokens visible, but the original documents hidden, we train these representations on real-world search engine interaction data with pairwise objectives, instilling the discriminative capability required to distinguish competing candidates for the purpose of ranking. In the third stage, we continue training the model directly on labeled ranking data, so that it learns to leverage the gist tokens to produce the listwise permutation both efficiently and accurately.

In this section, we evaluate the ranking effectiveness of GistRank . We rerank the top-100 passages retrieved by BM25 and report nDCG@10 on seven datasets, including the two TREC deep-learning sets DL19 and DL20 as well as five BEIR subsets covering diverse domains, namely TREC-COVID, DBPedia, SciFact, NFCorpus, and Touché. We compare against a broad set of baselines that spans pointwise, sliding-window, full-context, and embedding-based models, and further include two Qwen3-4B variants trained under full-context and summary-based settings. Finally, we report the nDCG@10 results for each subset, as well as the average performance across the seven datasets.

The results are presented in Table 2 . Despite compressing each passage into only a few gist tokens, GistRank achieves an average nDCG@10 of 59.17, ranking second among all evaluated methods and trailing the strongest baseline, FullRank 100 , by 0.89 points. On the in-domain TREC datasets, GistRank achieves the highest score on DL19 at 73.88 and the second-highest score on DL20 at 70.82. These results suggest that compact gist representations retain relevance information needed for effective ranking. Compared with the Qwen3-SFT-Full baselines built on the same backbone, GistRank improves average nDCG@10 by 1.37 points over sliding-window ranking and 2.00 points over full-list ranking, demonstrating that its compact representations support competitive effectiveness even when compared with methods that retain the original passage text. In Section 5.4 , we establish a more direct performance reference by employing a full-text rank slot variant based on the uncompressed outputs from Stage 2. The comparison with Qwen3-SFT-Summary further highlights the effectiveness of learned soft compression: GistRank exceeds the summary-based baselines by 6.83–7.65 points on average. This gap suggests that learned gist representations preserve ranking-relevant information more effectively than BM25-extracted summaries. On the out-of-domain five BEIR datasets, performance varies across domains, but GistRank remains competitive on Covid and DBPedia, achieving scores of 82.42 and 43.20, respectively. Its overall average also exceeds those of the evaluated baselines, although individual methods retain advantages on particular datasets. These results indicate that GistRank can significantly reduce ranking latency while still maintaining robust overall ranking performance.

The same distinction applies to privacy-facing, optimizer-state, and adapter uses of gradients. passages.text: Large scale language model (LLM) pretraining is increasingly bottlenecked by optimizer efficiency, driving optimizer design from vector-aware methods such as AdamW to matrix-aware methods. Matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon exploit matrix structure but treat layers independently, neglecting cross-layer correlations. Tensor-aware optimizers are therefore needed, yet existing ones rely on a matricization-based tensor algebra and remain restricted to shallow stacking and specific modules. In this paper, we propose TUON , a novel optimizer built on a transform-based tensor algebra derived from the Tensor-SVD (T-SVD). Unlike methods that polarize a globally unfolded matrix, TUON mixes layers via a unitary transform 𝑸 \bm{Q} and then polarizes each transformed slice, and inverts the transform to recover the update. This mix-then-separate strategy captures cross-layer correlations while preserving per-layer diversity, avoiding the structural dimension imbalance and cross-layer misalignment of unfolding. Thus it successfully scales to more layers and diverse modules beyond QKV. Theoretically, we prove that TUON performs steepest descent under a 𝑸 \bm{Q} -transformed tensor spectral norm, and identify its update as the tensor polar factor of the T-SVD. We further establish transform non-redundancy, norm and smoothness comparisons with Muon and TEON, and a convergence guarantee. Empirically, TUON improves consistently over Muon and TEON on GPT-124M/350M and Qwen-0.6B/4B, with ablations confirming the transformation mechanism, cross-layer structure beyond two-layer stacking, adaptability beyond QKV, and robustness to the polarization method.
